newsitem.title: JAPAN: Israel Treasury says slower growth may prompt cuts.
newsitem.headline: Israel Treasury says slower growth may prompt cuts.

text.p: The Israeli government may have to cut spending to rein in its budget deficit even if the economy grows by as much as three percent this year, a senior Treasury official said in Tokyo on Tuesday.
"What we are still concerned about is that the slowdown will affect the revenue side," Israeli Treasury Director-General David Brodet told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
Israel's 1997 budget calls for a deficit of 9.7 billion shekels, or 2.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). That projection is based on the economy growing by four percent this year.
But the current slowdown, driven by high interest rates, has raised questions about whether Israel's economy can grow that fast and whether spending cuts will be needed, Brodet said.
"If (growth) is between 3-4 percent, I still have the feeling that some adjustment in 1997 will be needed," he said.
Brodet said the level of inflation-adjusted interest rates in Israel is still "quite high", and said the central bank has room to ease further in April.
Tighter fiscal policy has taken some of the pressure off monetary policy, he said.
"Due to the fact that fiscal policy has become relatively tight, I think maybe we have to change the mixture between monetary and fiscal policy," he said.
Lower interest rates should help weaken the shekel, providing a boost to exports and ultimately to government revenues, he said.
Such an easing can be accomplished without jeopardising the government's 7-10 percent inflation target this year, Brodet said.
But he said inflation below seven percent would be undesirable this year, since it would involve an unacceptably drastic slowdown and increase in unemployment.
But the inflation target could be lowered gradually in 1998 and subsequent years, Brodet said.
"The gradual way is the recommended way for Israel in coming years," he said.
